title: Insights Teachers Should Share with Pupils (Part 1)
author: Jon Sellick
summary: Jon Sellick shares the first five entries from his student-facing guide '11 Ways to Be Brilliant at School', written directly to students rather than to teachers, with an explicit invitation for teachers to copy, adapt, or hand it straight to their classes. The guide splits its eleven tips into two categories -- 'Study Skills' and 'Life Habits' -- arguing both are equally important and mutually reinforcing, since habits like sleep and exercise directly enable the effectiveness of study techniques like spaced repetition. His first and, by his own account, single most important tip is sleep: he makes a detailed, sympathetic case that teenagers' difficulty waking up is biological rather than a character flaw, argues against the 'every waking hour' mentality of obsessive achievers, and gives a specific actionable target -- roughly nine hours a night, worked backward from a fixed school departure time -- while explicitly warning students against pulling all-nighters before exams. The post promises the remaining six tips (covering study techniques like spaced repetition, note-taking, and topic-sentence recognition, alongside further life habits like exercise and visualisation) in a follow-up newsletter.
points: Sellick's structural choice to split tips into 'Study Skill' and 'Life Habit' categories, explicitly framed as equally important and complementary, pushes back against a common assumption that only academic techniques matter for school success.

His sleep chapter directly reframes a common disciplinary narrative -- 'teenagers are lazy for not getting up' -- into a biological, non-blaming account, which changes the tone of a conversation that often becomes adversarial between students and adults.

The specific, calculable sleep target (roughly nine hours, calculated backward from a fixed school-departure time) turns vague sleep advice into an actionable number students can apply to their own schedule.

His explicit rejection of the 'every waking hour' achievement mentality -- arguing that hours spent awake are not a marker of success, and that sleep itself underpins the ability to do everything else well -- is a direct counter-message to common high-achiever burnout culture.
quotes: This week's newsletter is basically the first 5 tips from a guide I've written called '11 Ways to Be Brilliant at School'.
Being brilliant is hard. However, the good news is that you are already well on your way.
Your love of sleep and your difficulty getting out of bed in the morning does not mean you are lazy. It does not mean you are somehow deficient or not as good as others.
World class performers will tell you that they dedicate every waking hour to their craft.
The truth is that the time before we wake holds the key to our successes. It is sleep that matters most.
Let’s cut to the chase here: you need 9 hours of sleep every night.
This is the antithesis of everything this guide sets out to promote. So, understand that you should never pull an ‘all-nighter’. Ever.
